content:
Apple is vigorously fighting back against the Department of Justice's attempt to overturn a court ruling that allows the company to request documents from over a dozen federal agencies. Here's what's going on.

Some background

A few weeks ago, Apple won the right to request documents from 14 U.S. agencies as part of its defence against the DOJ's antitrust lawsuit filed against it in March 2024.

Those include the following agencies and departments:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

Apple's argument is that if it can demonstrate the federal government chose its products because of their privacy features, that evidence would support its claim that the practices the DOJ is challenging have legitimate justifications rather than being anticompetitive conduct.

After Apple won this dispute, the DOJ immediately filed a motion asking retired federal judge Jose Linares — who is serving as the special discovery master in the case — to reconsider his decision.

In complex cases involving large-scale document production, courts sometimes appoint special masters to handle narrower disputes to reduce the workload of the presiding judge. Special masters can be retired judges, practising attorneys, or other experts with relevant experience.

In its motion, the DOJ asked the court to overturn Apple's win on document production, arguing that Judge Linares applied the wrong legal standard by treating these agencies as parties to the case rather than non-parties entitled to greater document protections.

The DOJ also argued that Apple's requests would impose undue burdens on the agencies involved, citing 13 newly submitted declarations as support, and noted that the documents were of limited relevance because federal agencies are not "ordinary consumers."

"This motion falls apart at every turn"

Apple's response to the DOJ's motion has been made public, and the company pulled no punches in dismantling every single argument the DOJ raised to overturn the ruling.

Apple cited multiple prior cases, arguing that "the special master correctly applied the legal standard for party document production against federal agencies," and then systematically broke down the DOJ's arguments regarding undue burden and relevance.

In its conclusion, Apple said:

Per Judge Linares's schedule set on August 4, no further written submissions will be accepted, and it is now up to him to decide whether to maintain the original document production order or grant the DOJ's request for reconsideration.
